newsitem.title: USA: White House weighs initiative for Africa.
newsitem.headline: White House weighs initiative for Africa.

text.p: White House officials are working on a broad inititiative to help spur economic development and trade in Africa, an administration official said on Thursday.

"There is an increasing interest, a strongly developing interest in Africa within the administration," the official told a small business group. "There is a strong interest in making sure that we work with this continent to try to help development."
The official, who asked not to be identified, said the initiative would focus on trade liberalisation and economic reforms that would lower business costs and spur investment.

"There are elements of trade liberalisation that help open up domestic industries to competition, bring down costs and have wider ramifications that are useful to the entire economy," the official said.
Administration officials admit they do not have a lot of aid money so the initiative would have to focus on trade and private enterprise.

"The focus of this new initiative is taking more of a look at free market forces rather than having additional aid," the official said. "That approach also resonates more with some of our Republican friends in Congress."
A recent World Bank study said that protectionism costs Africa as much as $11 billion per year, an amount equal to the total external aid in 1991.

A report released last week by the U.S. Trade Representative's office on African policy said that although some countries liberalised investment policies to attract foreign money, many have restrictive policies, ineffecient public enterprises and legal systems that discourage private and foreign investment.

The administration official said the initiative on Africa is still being developed but it could include broading the General System of Preferences Programme (GSP), which allows certain goods from poor countries to enter the United States duty free.
"There is no question that this needs to be an initiative in which we open our markets," the official said.
He said he hoped the administration would unveil the initiative relatively soon.
"We're not talking about rolling this out a year and a half from now," he said.
Other administration officials said they hoped to have a package together by the time the leaders of the Group of Seven rich industrial nations hold their annual summit in Denver this summer.
Officials said the hope is to single out a few countries for special attention and then hold them up as examples of what can be accomplished through economic reforms and opening markets.
That approach seemed to work in Eastern Europe where the United States concentrated on helping Poland transfer from communism to a capitalist system.
